title: 1 tbsp ground flaxseed
evidence_note: Flaxseed is a reliable plant source of ALA omega-3 and fibre. Health Canada sets an adequate intake for ALA and for fibre. Grind it: whole seeds pass through undigested.

title: Chia, always soaked or in liquid
evidence_note: Adds fibre and ALA to oats, dahi or a shake. No separate health claim is made. Never eat it dry by the spoonful: it swells.
caution: Eat chia only mixed into liquid or soaked first.

title: A handful of nuts
evidence_note: Nuts and seeds are named plant protein foods in Health Canada's dietary guidelines. Walnuts add ALA; almonds add calcium and magnesium.

title: Pumpkin or hemp seeds as a topping
evidence_note: Adds zinc, magnesium, iron and protein to a meal. Nutrient values come from the CNF entries in this app. No health outcome is claimed.

title: Dahi or kefir daily
evidence_note: Gives protein, calcium and some B12 in a normal serving. It is also an easy way to close a protein gap. No claim is made about probiotics.

title: Fibre toward the daily target
evidence_note: Health Canada's adequate intake for adults aged 31 to 50 is 38 g a day for men and 25 g a day for women. The app shows fibre from the plan next to protein.

title: Water through the day
evidence_note: Health Canada's adequate intake for total water, including water from food, is 3.7 L a day for men and 2.7 L for women aged 31 to 50. Water is also the drink of choice in Canada's Food Guide.

title: Half the plate vegetables and fruit
evidence_note: Health Canada's dietary guidelines recommend filling half the plate with vegetables and fruit, a quarter with protein foods and a quarter with whole grains.

title: Plain or warm water on waking
evidence_note: Good for hydration. That is the only benefit; no detox effect. Strong here means the hydration advice, not any extra claim.

title: Lemon water
evidence_note: Fine for hydration and a little vitamin C. No evidence for other benefits. The acid is hard on tooth enamel, so rinse with plain water afterward.
caution: Rinse your mouth with plain water after drinking.

title: Jeera or ajwain water
evidence_note: A traditional digestive drink. There is little human evidence, so treat it as a preference.

title: Soaked fenugreek (methi) seeds or the soaking water
evidence_note: A meta-analysis of clinical trials found lower fasting glucose, 2-hour glucose and HbA1c, mostly in people with diabetes. The authors rated most of the trials as low quality, so the evidence is moderate at best.
caution: Anyone taking diabetes medication should ask a doctor first.

title: Detox drinks
evidence_note: The liver and kidneys do this work. No drink speeds it up. The app lists this so the claim is labelled honestly and not offered as a habit.

title: Soaking almonds overnight
evidence_note: A study of whole almonds found that soaking did not meaningfully lower phytate, and chopped almonds lost minerals when soaked. Soak them if you prefer the texture, not for health.

title: Soak rajma, chole, whole moong, urad or chana
evidence_note: Soaking for 8 to 12 hours cuts cooking time a lot. Discard the soaking water. Always boil rajma hard for 10 minutes when cooking.

title: Sprout moong or chana, then cook lightly
evidence_note: Sprouting starts 1 to 2 days ahead and adds volume. Protein stays about the same. Raw sprouts carry a food-safety risk, so steam or sauté them before eating.
caution: Cook sprouts before eating, especially for children, older adults and anyone pregnant.

title: Set dahi for tomorrow
evidence_note: Warm milk, a spoon of starter, 8 hours. Gives tomorrow's protein with no extra work.

title: Overnight oats or chia pudding
evidence_note: Zero morning effort and an easy high-protein breakfast with yoghurt or milk.

title: Marinate tofu or paneer
evidence_note: Gives the flavour that makes global and tikka-style recipes work. Two hours is enough, overnight is better.

title: Move frozen items to the fridge
evidence_note: Thawing overnight in the fridge is safer than on the counter and means dinner is ready to cook.
